q: The truth is, for the most part, it’s a sham. Expectations for student behavior in this day and age are knee-high to a five year old.

You’re asked to rely on one of the several trendy “research-based” classroom management systems your school has adopted that reject true accountability, replacing it with extrinsic rewards and appeasement.

Except for the occasional temporary improvement (e.g. students getting quiet or sitting up straight) that can happen in exchange for a reward or false praise—hence the “research”—behavior worsens over time.

All students need firmly established, nonnegotiable boundaries. If they don’t have them, in the form of clearly defined rules and their consequences, then they’ll push and probe and test until they find them.
Caring isn’t giving chance after chance. It isn’t looking the other way or excusing behavior you know is wrong. It isn’t pretending everything is okay while Rome burns.
You do right by students, and their families who have so much hope for them, by establishing boundaries that safeguard excellent teaching and inspired learning.
x: Argues that institutional talk of 'high expectations' is largely a sham as real behavior standards continue to erode.
Contends reward-based, 'research-based' classroom management systems worsen behavior over time despite occasional short-term compliance.
He argues this approach, dressed up as research-based, actually worsens behavior over time while punishing well-behaved students who quietly absorb the resulting disorder.

His counter-argument is that firm, clearly defined, consistently enforced boundaries are what make students feel safe and cared for, and that true caring means holding students accountable rather than repeatedly…
Redefines true caring as making hard, accountability-driven decisions rather than repeatedly excusing misbehavior.
Argues firm, consistently enforced boundaries make students feel safe and cared for, not oppressed.

t: A Super Easy Way To Lower Your Stress
q: It’s used by archers, golfers, surgeons, yoga teachers, and others whose performance is so directly linked to their ability to keep their composure.
The narrow passages of the nose force you to slow down your breathing, filling the lower half of your lungs and stimulating parasympathetic nerves that automatically calm the body.
It very effectively removes excitability from your classroom, which is one of the biggest causes of misbehavior. Students take their cue from you, and if you’re calm, they will be too.
Although it may take a few days to develop the habit of nasal breathing, you’ll find it delivering blessed relief within your first hour of practice.
It will show you just how profoundly a naturally calm demeanor positively influences those around you.
Your students. Your colleagues. Even the loved ones you go home to.
x: Linsin introduces nasal breathing—breathing exclusively through the nose except while talking or eating—as a simple, scientifically grounded technique for staying calm throughout the teaching day.
Explains that narrow nasal passages naturally slow breathing and engage the parasympathetic nervous system.

He also connects the practice to classroom management directly, noting that it discourages excessive narrating, reminding, and micromanaging of students, and that a calm teacher visibly transmits calm to the class.
Claims noticeable relief can occur within the very first hour of practicing the technique.

t: How To Respond After Losing Your Cool
q: You’re convinced that you’ve ruined everything, that you’ve undone all the influence, trust, and goodwill you’ve built up since the start of the year.
Although you may wince, it’s helpful to understand why you reacted the way you did. This alone goes a long way toward ensuring that it doesn’t happen again.
I messed up. It wasn’t okay how I reacted. It wasn’t okay that I didn’t follow through on my promise to protect your right to learn and enjoy being part of this class.
Second, students—and people in general—are quick to forgive those who openly admit their wrongdoings. It’s rare in this day and age, and thus more powerful and meaningful than ever.
Third, vulnerability makes you more likable. It makes you more authentic and your lessons more interesting, allowing you to build easy rapport with your students.
It will make you more confident and influential. It will make you more of the kind of leader your students will respect and admire.

t: How To Give Effective Praise: 6 Guidelines
q: Typically, praise is given far too frequently. Most classrooms are a constant stream of way-to-gos and good-jobs, regardless of accomplishment—or lack thereof.
It’s also often used dishonestly as a tool to manipulate students into desired behavior.
Praise should be directed not at the student(s) themselves—as in, “You’re an amazing writer!”—but at their accomplishment.
Praise that inspires students to greater levels of achievement is honest, specific, authentic (often subtle), and based not on natural ability, but on the process of learning, growing, and maturing.
It’s perfectly okay to let them wallow in their success without your input.

It supports a growth mindset. It drives students toward mastery and the profound intrinsic rewards of learning and acquiring skill, knowledge, and the confidence to tackle more and greater challenges with gusto.
x: Recommends directing praise at accomplishments rather than at the student's identity or innate ability.
Linsin, who says he's written about praise since 2009, warns against both overusing false, indiscriminate praise and swinging too far toward withholding it altogether.
